title: Why Invisible Flashes Shape Your Heart?
description:
Experimental Chronicle — Robert Zajonc (1968): Flashed Nonsense Words & Chinese Symbols — Why Mere Repetition Breeds Affection Without Memory!, grounded in Robert B. Zajonc (1968) (Journal of Personality and Social Psychology). Empirical findings show that folk proverbs contradicted each other — 'Familiarity breeds contempt' vs 'Absence makes the heart grow fonder' — until *1968 (Journal of Personality and Social Psychology Monograph Supplement), when University of Michigan psychologist Robert Zajonc tested pure, unrewarded repetition ('Mere Exposure')* across four completely different domains.

At the circuit level, this episode examines how primary visual cortex, amygdala, prefrontal cortex coordinate behavioral and neural responses, alongside evidence that first, Zajonc checked natural language frequencies: across cultures and languages, more frequently used words ('good', 'happy', 'clean', low numbers like 1 and 2) are overwhelmingly rated more positive than rare counterparts ('bad', 'sad', 'dirty').

Primary Peer-Reviewed Sources:
- Robert B. Zajonc (1968). Attitudinal effects of mere exposure. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/h0025848
- Richard L. Moreland, Robert B. Zajonc (1979). Exposure effects may not depend on stimulus recognition. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/0022-3514.37.6.1085
- S. Jay Samuels (1970). Recognition of Flashed Words by Children. Child Development. https://doi.org/10.2307/1127335

AI Disclosure: Visual reenactments, 3D anatomical models, and narration in this documentary Short were produced with AI synthesis tools from verified peer-reviewed sources.
